It was just another slow Tuesday at the skate shop—a day full of dust motes dancing in the shafts of sunlight slanting through the front windows, the hum of the mini fridge behind the counter, and the occasional clatter of a loosened wheel on the workbench. I was half-listening to an old mixtape and tightening trucks on a battered deck when the bell over the door jingled.

And that’s when she walked in.

Julie. I didn’t know her name yet, but I’d remember it for the rest of my life.

She stepped through the door like the world had been waiting for her to catch up, honey brown hair tucked behind one ear, a white tank top that hit just above the waistband of her strainingly tight jean shorts, and eyes that seemed to scan the room like she was already writing its story in her head. Not the usual kind of customer we got around here. Not unless you counted the huge dumptruck of an ass she carried behind her.

She walked past the long wall of decks like she belonged there—like maybe she rode every one of them in a dream. And then she looked right at me and smiled.
